# A New Tyrannosaurus Species is Described

Scientists have identified a new species of tyrannosaur from fossils found in western New Mexico. The dinosaur has been named _Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis_. Although it lived many millions of years before _T. rex_, it was closely related to it and around the same size.

[![Image 3: Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis life reconstruction.](https://blog.everythingdinosaur.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/NM-tyrannosaur-Sergey-Krasovskiy-1.jpg)](http://blog.everythingdinosaur.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/NM-tyrannosaur-Sergey-Krasovskiy-1.jpg)

_A life reconstruction of Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis with the contemporaneous chasmosaur Sierraceratops in the background. Picture credit: Sergey Krasovskiy._

### _Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis_

The study, published in “Scientific Reports” postulates that the ancestors of _T. rex_ originated in southern Laramidia. Where and when the tyrannosaur lineage that includes _T. rex_ and its closest relatives evolved remains unclear. It had been thought that these theropods originated in Asia, or perhaps at more northerly latitudes of Laramidia. The identification of fossils representing a giant, 12-metre-plus tyrannosaur suggests that large-bodied, apex predators evolved alongside other exceptionally large dinosaurs at lower latitudes.

The researchers examined a partial skull (NMMNH P-3698), that had been excavated from a location in Sierra County, New Mexico. The fossil material consisted of a right postorbital and squamosal, along with a left palatine, a fragmentary maxilla and elements from the lower jaws including the left dentary. The fossils come from Hall Lake Formation (McRae Group). Uranium to lead (U/Pb) isotope analysis of a layer some thirty metres below the tyrannosaur fossil site is dated to 73.2 mya plus or minus 0.7 million years. This indicates that _Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis_ predates _T. rex_ by approximately 6-7 million years.

[![Image 4: Skull bones of Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis.](https://blog.everythingdinosaur.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/F2-Tyrannoatrox-Figure-2-March-23.jpg)](http://blog.everythingdinosaur.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/F2-Tyrannoatrox-Figure-2-March-23.jpg)

_Cranial elements of Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis (NMMNH P-3698). Right postorbital in (A), lateral view; (B), medial view; (C), dorsal view. Right squamosal in (D), lateral view; (E), medial view; (F), ventral view. Note scale bars = 10 cm. Picture credit: Dalman et al._

The skull bones, previously assigned to _T. rex_ are currently on display at the New Mexico Museum of Natural History & Science (NMMNHS).

[![Image 5: Views of the Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis mandible](https://blog.everythingdinosaur.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/F3-New-Figure-3-mandible.jpg)](http://blog.everythingdinosaur.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/F3-New-Figure-3-mandible.jpg)

_The left dentary of Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis (NMMNH P-3698) in media view (A), lateral view (B) and dorsal view (C). The right spenial in medial view (D) and (E) the right angular in medial view. The right prearticular is shown in medial view (F). Note scale bar = 20 cm. Picture credit: Dalman et al._

### Older and More Primitive than _Tyrannosaurus rex_

While the new discovery predates _T. rex_, the paper notes that subtle differences in the jaw bones make it unlikely that _T. mcraeensis_ was a direct ancestor. However, it is assigned to the Tyrannosaurini tribe, which is defined by the authors as the last common ancestor of the Asian _Tarbosaurus bataar_ and _Tyrannosaurus rex_ and all its descendants.

Contributing authors on the study include researchers from the University of Bath (UK), NMMNHS, University of Utah, The George Washington University, Harrisburg University, Penn State Lehigh Valley, and the University of Alberta.

Ironically, it was the examination of horned dinosaur fossils from the same palaeoenvironment that led to the discovery of a new Tyrannosaurus species. In 2013, then-student Sebastian Dalman began to re-examine ceratopsian fossils, it led to a broader rethink about the dinosaur fauna associated with the McRae Group.

Dalman commented:

_“I started working on this project in 2013 with co-author Steve Jasinski and soon we started to suspect we were on to something new.”_

### Careful Comparison with _T. rex_ Skull Fossils

Analysis of the skull material revealed subtle, but unique traits relating to their morphology and articulation. Careful comparison with _T. rex_ skull fossils led the research team to conclude that these bones did not represent _Tyrannosaurus rex_. This was something new.

[![Image 6: Comparing skull bones of T. mcraeensis and T. rex.](https://blog.everythingdinosaur.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/F6-New-figure-6-atrox-compare.jpg)](http://blog.everythingdinosaur.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/F6-New-figure-6-atrox-compare.jpg)

_Comparing skull bones of the newly described Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis and Tyrannosaurus rex. Variation in the postorbitals (A–F), dentaries (G–K) and splenials (M–Q) of Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis (A, G, M) and Tyrannosaurus rex (B–F, H–L, N–Q). Scale bars = 10 cm. Picture credit: Dalman et al._

As _T. rex_ is known from multiple individuals, it is possible to show that _T. mcraeensis_ lies outside of the range of individual variation seen in _T. rex_.

Co-author of the paper, Dr Anthony Fiorillo, Executive Director of NMMNHS explained:

_“New Mexicans have always known our state is special, now we know that New Mexico has been a special place for tens of millions of years. This study delivers on the mission of this museum through the science-based investigation of the history of life on our planet.”_

Size estimates for _Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis_ put it in the same bracket as the famous and geologically younger _T. rex_. It is thought to have measured around twelve metres in length.

Fellow author of the paper, Dr Nick Longrich (Milner Centre for Evolution at the University of Bath) added:

_“The differences are subtle, but that’s typically the case in closely related species. Evolution slowly causes mutations to build up over millions of years, causing species to look subtly different over time.”_

### _Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis_ and the Origins of _T. rex_

The identification of a new Tyrannosaurus from New Mexico raises the intriguing possibility that there are several more new tyrannosaur discoveries yet to be made.

Co-author Dr Spencer Lucas (Palaeontology Curator at the NMMNHS) stated:

_“Once again, the extent and scientific importance of New Mexico’s dinosaur fossils becomes clear. Many new dinosaurs remain to be discovered in the state, both in the rocks and in museum drawers!”_

_Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis_ expands our understanding of tyrannosaurs in several ways. Firstly, it suggests that the apex predators lived in what is now the southern United States at least 72 million years ago. Secondly, the Tyrannosaurus genus likely originated in southern North America then later expanded into much of the western portion of the continent.

Phylogenetic analysis supports this hypothesis. The analysis places _T. mcraeensis_ as sister taxon to _T. rex_ and suggests the Tyrannosaurini tribe originated in southern Laramidia.

[![Image 7: Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis phylogeny and size comparison with T. rex.](https://blog.everythingdinosaur.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/new-tyrannosaur-phylogeny.jpg)](http://blog.everythingdinosaur.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/new-tyrannosaur-phylogeny.jpg)

_Size, relationships and biogeography of Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis. (A), relative sizes of Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis (NMMNH P-3698) and Tyrannosaurus rex known as “Sue” (FMNH PR 2081) and the type specimen (CM 9380). An evolutionary tree based on Bayesian tip-dated phylogeny and biogeographic analysis. Picture credit: Dalman et al._

### _Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis_ Raises More Questions

The skull fossils assigned to _T. mcraeensis_ suggest that larger, more robust and powerful tyrannosaurs evolved in the southern United States compared to the smaller and more primitive tyrannosaurs found further north.

For reasons as yet unknown, dinosaurs may have evolved to larger sizes in lower latitudes in North America. This body condition pattern is not seen in modern mammals. This newly described tyrannosaur was part of an ecosystem dominated by super-sized dinosaurs. For example, the giant chasmosaur _Sierraceratops turneri_ was contemporaneous. In addition, the titanosaur Alamosaurus and an as yet, undescribed giant hadrosaur shared this palaeoenvironment.

[![Image 8: Dinosaurs of the Hall Lake Formation.](https://blog.everythingdinosaur.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Hall-Lake-dinosaurs-1.jpg)](http://blog.everythingdinosaur.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Hall-Lake-dinosaurs-1.jpg)

_Dinosaurs of the Campanian-Maastrichtian Hall Lake Formation. Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis (NMMNH P-3698), the horned dinosaur Sierraceratops turneri, a giant but as yet undescribed hadrosaurid and the titanosaur Alamosaurus. Picture credit: Dalman et al._

Giant tyrannosaurs were able to spread north during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous. The reasons for this migration remain unclear. Perhaps the northward spread of giant herbivores such as Triceratops and Torosaurus created a food source that could be exploited by the very biggest tyrannosaurs.

The scientific paper: _“A giant tyrannosaur from the Campanian–Maastrichtian of southern North America and the evolution of tyrannosaurid gigantism”_ by Sebastian G. Dalman, Mark A. Loewen, R. Alexander Pyron, Steven E. Jasinski, D. Edward Malinzak, Spencer G. Lucas, Anthony R. Fiorillo,  
Philip J. Currie and Nicholas R. Longrich published in Scientific Reports.

# A New Tyrannosaurus Species is Described

Scientists have identified a new species of tyrannosaur from fossils found in western New Mexico. The dinosaur has been named _Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis_. Although it lived many millions of years before _T. rex_, it was closely related to it and around the same size.

[![Image 3: Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis life reconstruction.](https://blog.everythingdinosaur.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/NM-tyrannosaur-Sergey-Krasovskiy-1.jpg)](http://blog.everythingdinosaur.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/NM-tyrannosaur-Sergey-Krasovskiy-1.jpg)

_A life reconstruction of Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis with the contemporaneous chasmosaur Sierraceratops in the background. Picture credit: Sergey Krasovskiy._

### _Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis_

The study, published in “Scientific Reports” postulates that the ancestors of _T. rex_ originated in southern Laramidia. Where and when the tyrannosaur lineage that includes _T. rex_ and its closest relatives evolved remains unclear. It had been thought that these theropods originated in Asia, or perhaps at more northerly latitudes of Laramidia. The identification of fossils representing a giant, 12-metre-plus tyrannosaur suggests that large-bodied, apex predators evolved alongside other exceptionally large dinosaurs at lower latitudes.

The researchers examined a partial skull (NMMNH P-3698), that had been excavated from a location in Sierra County, New Mexico. The fossil material consisted of a right postorbital and squamosal, along with a left palatine, a fragmentary maxilla and elements from the lower jaws including the left dentary. The fossils come from Hall Lake Formation (McRae Group). Uranium to lead (U/Pb) isotope analysis of a layer some thirty metres below the tyrannosaur fossil site is dated to 73.2 mya plus or minus 0.7 million years. This indicates that _Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis_ predates _T. rex_ by approximately 6-7 million years.

[![Image 4: Skull bones of Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis.](https://blog.everythingdinosaur.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/F2-Tyrannoatrox-Figure-2-March-23.jpg)](http://blog.everythingdinosaur.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/F2-Tyrannoatrox-Figure-2-March-23.jpg)

_Cranial elements of Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis (NMMNH P-3698). Right postorbital in (A), lateral view; (B), medial view; (C), dorsal view. Right squamosal in (D), lateral view; (E), medial view; (F), ventral view. Note scale bars = 10 cm. Picture credit: Dalman et al._

The skull bones, previously assigned to _T. rex_ are currently on display at the New Mexico Museum of Natural History & Science (NMMNHS).

[![Image 5: Views of the Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis mandible](https://blog.everythingdinosaur.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/F3-New-Figure-3-mandible.jpg)](http://blog.everythingdinosaur.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/F3-New-Figure-3-mandible.jpg)

_The left dentary of Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis (NMMNH P-3698) in media view (A), lateral view (B) and dorsal view (C). The right spenial in medial view (D) and (E) the right angular in medial view. The right prearticular is shown in medial view (F). Note scale bar = 20 cm. Picture credit: Dalman et al._

### Older and More Primitive than _Tyrannosaurus rex_

While the new discovery predates _T. rex_, the paper notes that subtle differences in the jaw bones make it unlikely that _T. mcraeensis_ was a direct ancestor. However, it is assigned to the Tyrannosaurini tribe, which is defined by the authors as the last common ancestor of the Asian _Tarbosaurus bataar_ and _Tyrannosaurus rex_ and all its descendants.

Contributing authors on the study include researchers from the University of Bath (UK), NMMNHS, University of Utah, The George Washington University, Harrisburg University, Penn State Lehigh Valley, and the University of Alberta.

Ironically, it was the examination of horned dinosaur fossils from the same palaeoenvironment that led to the discovery of a new Tyrannosaurus species. In 2013, then-student Sebastian Dalman began to re-examine ceratopsian fossils, it led to a broader rethink about the dinosaur fauna associated with the McRae Group.

Dalman commented:

_“I started working on this project in 2013 with co-author Steve Jasinski and soon we started to suspect we were on to something new.”_

### Careful Comparison with _T. rex_ Skull Fossils

Analysis of the skull material revealed subtle, but unique traits relating to their morphology and articulation. Careful comparison with _T. rex_ skull fossils led the research team to conclude that these bones did not represent _Tyrannosaurus rex_. This was something new.

[![Image 6: Comparing skull bones of T. mcraeensis and T. rex.](https://blog.everythingdinosaur.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/F6-New-figure-6-atrox-compare.jpg)](http://blog.everythingdinosaur.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/F6-New-figure-6-atrox-compare.jpg)

_Comparing skull bones of the newly described Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis and Tyrannosaurus rex. Variation in the postorbitals (A–F), dentaries (G–K) and splenials (M–Q) of Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis (A, G, M) and Tyrannosaurus rex (B–F, H–L, N–Q). Scale bars = 10 cm. Picture credit: Dalman et al._

As _T. rex_ is known from multiple individuals, it is possible to show that _T. mcraeensis_ lies outside of the range of individual variation seen in _T. rex_.

Co-author of the paper, Dr Anthony Fiorillo, Executive Director of NMMNHS explained:

_“New Mexicans have always known our state is special, now we know that New Mexico has been a special place for tens of millions of years. This study delivers on the mission of this museum through the science-based investigation of the history of life on our planet.”_

Size estimates for _Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis_ put it in the same bracket as the famous and geologically younger _T. rex_. It is thought to have measured around twelve metres in length.

Fellow author of the paper, Dr Nick Longrich (Milner Centre for Evolution at the University of Bath) added:

_“The differences are subtle, but that’s typically the case in closely related species. Evolution slowly causes mutations to build up over millions of years, causing species to look subtly different over time.”_

### _Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis_ and the Origins of _T. rex_

The identification of a new Tyrannosaurus from New Mexico raises the intriguing possibility that there are several more new tyrannosaur discoveries yet to be made.

Co-author Dr Spencer Lucas (Palaeontology Curator at the NMMNHS) stated:

_“Once again, the extent and scientific importance of New Mexico’s dinosaur fossils becomes clear. Many new dinosaurs remain to be discovered in the state, both in the rocks and in museum drawers!”_

_Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis_ expands our understanding of tyrannosaurs in several ways. Firstly, it suggests that the apex predators lived in what is now the southern United States at least 72 million years ago. Secondly, the Tyrannosaurus genus likely originated in southern North America then later expanded into much of the western portion of the continent.

Phylogenetic analysis supports this hypothesis. The analysis places _T. mcraeensis_ as sister taxon to _T. rex_ and suggests the Tyrannosaurini tribe originated in southern Laramidia.

[![Image 7: Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis phylogeny and size comparison with T. rex.](https://blog.everythingdinosaur.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/new-tyrannosaur-phylogeny.jpg)](http://blog.everythingdinosaur.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/new-tyrannosaur-phylogeny.jpg)

_Size, relationships and biogeography of Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis. (A), relative sizes of Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis (NMMNH P-3698) and Tyrannosaurus rex known as “Sue” (FMNH PR 2081) and the type specimen (CM 9380). An evolutionary tree based on Bayesian tip-dated phylogeny and biogeographic analysis. Picture credit: Dalman et al._

### _Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis_ Raises More Questions

The skull fossils assigned to _T. mcraeensis_ suggest that larger, more robust and powerful tyrannosaurs evolved in the southern United States compared to the smaller and more primitive tyrannosaurs found further north.

For reasons as yet unknown, dinosaurs may have evolved to larger sizes in lower latitudes in North America. This body condition pattern is not seen in modern mammals. This newly described tyrannosaur was part of an ecosystem dominated by super-sized dinosaurs. For example, the giant chasmosaur _Sierraceratops turneri_ was contemporaneous. In addition, the titanosaur Alamosaurus and an as yet, undescribed giant hadrosaur shared this palaeoenvironment.

[![Image 8: Dinosaurs of the Hall Lake Formation.](https://blog.everythingdinosaur.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Hall-Lake-dinosaurs-1.jpg)](http://blog.everythingdinosaur.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Hall-Lake-dinosaurs-1.jpg)

_Dinosaurs of the Campanian-Maastrichtian Hall Lake Formation. Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis (NMMNH P-3698), the horned dinosaur Sierraceratops turneri, a giant but as yet undescribed hadrosaurid and the titanosaur Alamosaurus. Picture credit: Dalman et al._

Giant tyrannosaurs were able to spread north during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous. The reasons for this migration remain unclear. Perhaps the northward spread of giant herbivores such as Triceratops and Torosaurus created a food source that could be exploited by the very biggest tyrannosaurs.

# Meet Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis: the Newest Species of Giant Tyrannosaur

In what has already become a fascinating year for paleontology, Tyrannosaurus gains a second species that hints at the origin of these gigantic predators

*    Post author  By [maxsblogosaurus](https://maxs-blogo-saurus.com/author/maxsblogosaurus/)
*    Post date January 12, 2024
*   6 Comments on Meet Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis: the Newest Species of Giant Tyrannosaur

![Image 1](https://maxs-blogo-saurus.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/re.jpeg?w=800)

_Tyrannosaurus_ has kicked off the new year with an absolute bang! Perhaps it was very dedicated to its resolutions?

Just over a week ago, on January 3 rd, paleontologists Nicholas Longrich and Evan Saitta published an examination of the Tyrannosaurid _Nanotyrannus_ and its taxonomic status. To summarize, they believed that the teenage tyrant was a valid genus and not a teenage _Tyrannosaurus rex_, the prevailing view in paleontology. While their study presented interesting arguments, including a new specimen of a juvenile Tyrannosaur, many individuals – including myself – considered the publication more of a review and insufficient to settle the debate. (For more information, read “[The Pipe Dream of _Nanotyrannus_ Reaches New Heights: Comments on Longrich & Saitta 2024](https://maxs-blogo-saurus.com/2024/01/04/the-pipe-dream-of-nanotyrannus-reaches-new-heights-comments-on-longrich-saitta-2024/)”).

It appears that Longrich is not very patient because it only took him 8 days to publish another study related to _Tyrannosaurus!_ This time, Longrich (and a larger team of researchers, including lead author Sebastian Dalman and legendary paleontologist Phil Currie) have introduced a new controversy to _Tyrannosaurus:_ a potential second species.

In 1983, a massive jawbone assigned to _Tyrannosaurus rex_ emerged from the Hall Lake Formation of New Mexico _._ In subsequent years, additional dinosaur fossils – including skull fragments from the same _Tyrannosaurus,_ Ceratopsian skeletons, and leg bones of both a sauropod and a large hadrosaur – would be found in Hall Lake deposits. The jaw of _Tyrannosaurus,_ specimen NMMNH P-3698, would be displayed at the New Mexico Museum of Natural History and Science for all to see, believed to be an inconsequential fossil for the taxonomy of its genus…

![Image 2](https://maxs-blogo-saurus.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/image-21.png?w=1001)

NMMNH P-3698, The jawbone of a new _Tyrannosaurus_ species. ©[Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/science/scientists-conclude-new-mexico-fossil-is-new-tyrannosaurus-species-2024-01-11/)

Until Dalman came along, that is. A thorough re-examination of NMMNH P-3698 led Dalman to conclude that it represented a distinct species from _Tyrannosaurus rex,_ known as _Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis[**[i]**](https://maxs-blogo-saurus.com/2024/01/12/meet-tyrannosaurus-mcraeensis-the-newest-species-of-giant-tyrannosaur/#\_edn1)._ The name _mcraeensis_ is surprisingly not dedicated to any individual involved in the study, instead stemming from the McRae Formation, which contains the Hall Lake subgroup. Many subtle anatomical differences between _T. mcraeensis_ and other _T. rex_ fossils were noted, though variation between individuals may explain many of these features away (why does [that sound familiar](https://maxs-blogo-saurus.com/2022/03/13/the-tyrannosaurus-trifecta-questions-regarding-t-rexs-species-split/)?). Some paleontologists, including Tyrannosaur expert Thomas Carr[[ii]](https://maxs-blogo-saurus.com/2024/01/12/meet-tyrannosaurus-mcraeensis-the-newest-species-of-giant-tyrannosaur/#_edn2), have already noted that NMMNH P-3698 doesn’t exhibit any features that vary drastically from _T. rex,_ so these traits may not be suitable for diagnosing a new species.

The age of _T. mcraeensis_ is however far more interesting. _T. rex_ was believed to have appeared in the later portion of the Maastrichtian Stage during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 68 million years ago. Hall Lake fossils, once thought to have fallen within this time range, were recently found to be approximately 73.2 million years old[[iii]](https://maxs-blogo-saurus.com/2024/01/12/meet-tyrannosaurus-mcraeensis-the-newest-species-of-giant-tyrannosaur/#_edn3). Using the distance of _T. mcraeensis’_ fossils relative to the sediments used to calculate this date, Dalman’s paper concludes that the site containing _T. mcraeensis_ was likely between 72.7 and 70.9 million years old.

If true, this discovery may rewrite our knowledge of _Tyrannosaurus_ evolution. Paleontologists have theorized that the Tyrannosaur subfamily Tyrannosaurini – which includes massive, late-stage genera like _Tyrannosaurus_ and the Asian _Tarbosaurus_ and _Zhuchengtyrannus_– originated in Asia and later dispersed to North America[[iv]](https://maxs-blogo-saurus.com/2024/01/12/meet-tyrannosaurus-mcraeensis-the-newest-species-of-giant-tyrannosaur/#_edn4). This theory is rooted in the age of the respective Tyrannosaurines, with _Zhuchengtyrannus_ and _Tarbosaurus_ appearing earlier in the fossil record than their close relative _Tyrannosaurus._ As the Tyrannosaurines moved to North America during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous approximately 69-68 million years ago, they replaced endemic Tyrannosaurids like _Albertosaurus,_ paving the way for _Tyrannosaurus rex_ to evolve.

![Image 3](https://maxs-blogo-saurus.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/image-23.png?w=1024)

A handful of derived Tyrannosaurids, including the key genera of Tyranosaurini: _Tyrannosaurus, Tarbosaurus, and Zhuchengtyrannus._©[pgr14art](https://www.facebook.com/pgr14art/photos/a.2369253623320824/2893374870908694/?type=3)

The discovery of an older _Tyrannosaurus_ species in New Mexico could refute this notion. If _Tyrannosaurus_ evolved simultaneously with the Asian Tyrannosaurines, the genus probably originated from North America instead of Asia. This scenario raises many questions regarding the dispersal patterns of Tyrannosaurini _._ Were other Tyrannosauids from North America, like _Lythronax_ and _Daspletosaurus,_ also part of the lineage? If there were large Tyrannosaurines in Asia and North America 72 million years ago, when and where did the lineage first appear? If they originated in southern North America, why don’t we find their fossils in northern areas like Montana and Alberta until the Late Maastrichtian? If _Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis_– or something like it – dispersed into Asia during the Campanian and diversified into _Zhuchengtyrannus_ and _Tarbosaurus,_ why did it not spread to the rest of North America at this time?

For now, these questions remain unanswered.

The idea that a second _Tyrannosaurus_ species may have existed isn’t new. In 2022, Paleontologist Greg Paul famously published a theory proposing a split of _Tyrannosaurus rex_ into three separate species: _T. rex, T. imperator,_ and _T. regina._ The general perception of this theory at the time was that, while these were very cool names to give the species, the proposed anatomical evidence to justify this divide was insufficient.

While most paleontologists agree that more species of _Tyrannosaurus_ may have existed _,_ no study has created a solid case for one – until now. While the study isn’t perfect (I’d love supplementary radiometric dating from the specific site where the fossils of _T. mcraeensis_ come from), the proposed age of the newest Tyrannosaur is perhaps the best evidence presented to justify a new species. I’m sure a counter argument will be published soon. For now, we can enjoy a second species of _Tyrannosaurus_ with a real case to be valid!

![Image 4](https://maxs-blogo-saurus.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/image-22.png?w=800)

©[Sergey Krasovskiy](https://twitter.com/TM9380/status/1745484246574113188)

**A few other things to note:**

*   Some online sources have connected _T. mcraeensis_ to “_Alamotyrannus,”_ a dubious genus of Tyrannosaur known from fossils found in New Mexico. This information is incorrect, as the proposed fossils of _Alamotyrannus_ are separate from the ones used to describe _T. mcraeensis._
*   While the remains of _T. mcraeensis_ are fragmentary, the size of the dentary indicates that it may have been longer than Scotty, the largest known specimen of _Tyrannosaurus rex!_
*   _Mcraeensis_ is spelt with two e’s. 
*   The name _Mcraeensis_ is admittedly terrible. Most hostility from paleo-twitter has stemmed from the name itself instead of the notion of a second _Tyrannosaurus_ species. If the research team wanted a better name, they should have used the [advice given by Max’s Blogosaurus!](https://maxs-blogo-saurus.com/2023/12/29/they-named-a-dinosaur-gremlin-slobodorum-a-case-study-in-pop-culture-dinosaur-names/)

# Meet Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis: the Newest Species of Giant Tyrannosaur

In what has already become a fascinating year for paleontology, Tyrannosaurus gains a second species that hints at the origin of these gigantic predators

*    Post author  By [maxsblogosaurus](https://maxs-blogo-saurus.com/author/maxsblogosaurus/)
*    Post date January 12, 2024
*   6 Comments on Meet Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis: the Newest Species of Giant Tyrannosaur

![Image 1](https://maxs-blogo-saurus.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/re.jpeg?w=800)

_Tyrannosaurus_ has kicked off the new year with an absolute bang! Perhaps it was very dedicated to its resolutions?

Just over a week ago, on January 3 rd, paleontologists Nicholas Longrich and Evan Saitta published an examination of the Tyrannosaurid _Nanotyrannus_ and its taxonomic status. To summarize, they believed that the teenage tyrant was a valid genus and not a teenage _Tyrannosaurus rex_, the prevailing view in paleontology. While their study presented interesting arguments, including a new specimen of a juvenile Tyrannosaur, many individuals – including myself – considered the publication more of a review and insufficient to settle the debate. (For more information, read “[The Pipe Dream of _Nanotyrannus_ Reaches New Heights: Comments on Longrich & Saitta 2024](https://maxs-blogo-saurus.com/2024/01/04/the-pipe-dream-of-nanotyrannus-reaches-new-heights-comments-on-longrich-saitta-2024/)”).

It appears that Longrich is not very patient because it only took him 8 days to publish another study related to _Tyrannosaurus!_ This time, Longrich (and a larger team of researchers, including lead author Sebastian Dalman and legendary paleontologist Phil Currie) have introduced a new controversy to _Tyrannosaurus:_ a potential second species.

In 1983, a massive jawbone assigned to _Tyrannosaurus rex_ emerged from the Hall Lake Formation of New Mexico _._ In subsequent years, additional dinosaur fossils – including skull fragments from the same _Tyrannosaurus,_ Ceratopsian skeletons, and leg bones of both a sauropod and a large hadrosaur – would be found in Hall Lake deposits. The jaw of _Tyrannosaurus,_ specimen NMMNH P-3698, would be displayed at the New Mexico Museum of Natural History and Science for all to see, believed to be an inconsequential fossil for the taxonomy of its genus…

![Image 2](https://maxs-blogo-saurus.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/image-21.png?w=1001)

NMMNH P-3698, The jawbone of a new _Tyrannosaurus_ species. ©[Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/science/scientists-conclude-new-mexico-fossil-is-new-tyrannosaurus-species-2024-01-11/)

Until Dalman came along, that is. A thorough re-examination of NMMNH P-3698 led Dalman to conclude that it represented a distinct species from _Tyrannosaurus rex,_ known as _Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis[**[i]**](https://maxs-blogo-saurus.com/2024/01/12/meet-tyrannosaurus-mcraeensis-the-newest-species-of-giant-tyrannosaur/#\_edn1)._ The name _mcraeensis_ is surprisingly not dedicated to any individual involved in the study, instead stemming from the McRae Formation, which contains the Hall Lake subgroup. Many subtle anatomical differences between _T. mcraeensis_ and other _T. rex_ fossils were noted, though variation between individuals may explain many of these features away (why does [that sound familiar](https://maxs-blogo-saurus.com/2022/03/13/the-tyrannosaurus-trifecta-questions-regarding-t-rexs-species-split/)?). Some paleontologists, including Tyrannosaur expert Thomas Carr[[ii]](https://maxs-blogo-saurus.com/2024/01/12/meet-tyrannosaurus-mcraeensis-the-newest-species-of-giant-tyrannosaur/#_edn2), have already noted that NMMNH P-3698 doesn’t exhibit any features that vary drastically from _T. rex,_ so these traits may not be suitable for diagnosing a new species.

The age of _T. mcraeensis_ is however far more interesting. _T. rex_ was believed to have appeared in the later portion of the Maastrichtian Stage during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 68 million years ago. Hall Lake fossils, once thought to have fallen within this time range, were recently found to be approximately 73.2 million years old[[iii]](https://maxs-blogo-saurus.com/2024/01/12/meet-tyrannosaurus-mcraeensis-the-newest-species-of-giant-tyrannosaur/#_edn3). Using the distance of _T. mcraeensis’_ fossils relative to the sediments used to calculate this date, Dalman’s paper concludes that the site containing _T. mcraeensis_ was likely between 72.7 and 70.9 million years old.

If true, this discovery may rewrite our knowledge of _Tyrannosaurus_ evolution. Paleontologists have theorized that the Tyrannosaur subfamily Tyrannosaurini – which includes massive, late-stage genera like _Tyrannosaurus_ and the Asian _Tarbosaurus_ and _Zhuchengtyrannus_– originated in Asia and later dispersed to North America[[iv]](https://maxs-blogo-saurus.com/2024/01/12/meet-tyrannosaurus-mcraeensis-the-newest-species-of-giant-tyrannosaur/#_edn4). This theory is rooted in the age of the respective Tyrannosaurines, with _Zhuchengtyrannus_ and _Tarbosaurus_ appearing earlier in the fossil record than their close relative _Tyrannosaurus._ As the Tyrannosaurines moved to North America during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous approximately 69-68 million years ago, they replaced endemic Tyrannosaurids like _Albertosaurus,_ paving the way for _Tyrannosaurus rex_ to evolve.

![Image 3](https://maxs-blogo-saurus.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/image-23.png?w=1024)

A handful of derived Tyrannosaurids, including the key genera of Tyranosaurini: _Tyrannosaurus, Tarbosaurus, and Zhuchengtyrannus._©[pgr14art](https://www.facebook.com/pgr14art/photos/a.2369253623320824/2893374870908694/?type=3)

The discovery of an older _Tyrannosaurus_ species in New Mexico could refute this notion. If _Tyrannosaurus_ evolved simultaneously with the Asian Tyrannosaurines, the genus probably originated from North America instead of Asia. This scenario raises many questions regarding the dispersal patterns of Tyrannosaurini _._ Were other Tyrannosauids from North America, like _Lythronax_ and _Daspletosaurus,_ also part of the lineage? If there were large Tyrannosaurines in Asia and North America 72 million years ago, when and where did the lineage first appear? If they originated in southern North America, why don’t we find their fossils in northern areas like Montana and Alberta until the Late Maastrichtian? If _Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis_– or something like it – dispersed into Asia during the Campanian and diversified into _Zhuchengtyrannus_ and _Tarbosaurus,_ why did it not spread to the rest of North America at this time?

For now, these questions remain unanswered.

The idea that a second _Tyrannosaurus_ species may have existed isn’t new. In 2022, Paleontologist Greg Paul famously published a theory proposing a split of _Tyrannosaurus rex_ into three separate species: _T. rex, T. imperator,_ and _T. regina._ The general perception of this theory at the time was that, while these were very cool names to give the species, the proposed anatomical evidence to justify this divide was insufficient.

While most paleontologists agree that more species of _Tyrannosaurus_ may have existed _,_ no study has created a solid case for one – until now. While the study isn’t perfect (I’d love supplementary radiometric dating from the specific site where the fossils of _T. mcraeensis_ come from), the proposed age of the newest Tyrannosaur is perhaps the best evidence presented to justify a new species. I’m sure a counter argument will be published soon. For now, we can enjoy a second species of _Tyrannosaurus_ with a real case to be valid!

![Image 4](https://maxs-blogo-saurus.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/image-22.png?w=800)

©[Sergey Krasovskiy](https://twitter.com/TM9380/status/1745484246574113188)

**A few other things to note:**

*   Some online sources have connected _T. mcraeensis_ to “_Alamotyrannus,”_ a dubious genus of Tyrannosaur known from fossils found in New Mexico. This information is incorrect, as the proposed fossils of _Alamotyrannus_ are separate from the ones used to describe _T. mcraeensis._
*   While the remains of _T. mcraeensis_ are fragmentary, the size of the dentary indicates that it may have been longer than Scotty, the largest known specimen of _Tyrannosaurus rex!_
*   _Mcraeensis_ is spelt with two e’s. 
*   The name _Mcraeensis_ is admittedly terrible. Most hostility from paleo-twitter has stemmed from the name itself instead of the notion of a second _Tyrannosaurus_ species. If the research team wanted a better name, they should have used the [advice given by Max’s Blogosaurus!](https://maxs-blogo-saurus.com/2023/12/29/they-named-a-dinosaur-gremlin-slobodorum-a-case-study-in-pop-culture-dinosaur-names/)

# Types of Tyrannosaur Dinosaurs and the Origins of T. rex

There was much more to the tyrannosaur family than _Tyrannosaurus rex_. Learn about the different types of tyrannosaur dinosaurs, where they lived, how they evolved, and how early feathered relatives eventually led to the giant bone-crushing predators of the Late Cretaceous.

_Article written by: [Jayson Kowinsky, The Fossilguy](https://www.fossilguy.com/author.htm)_

| Published August 10, 2015 (Updated: 01/27/2026)

![Image 8: Tyrannosaur size comparison showing T. rex and other tyrannosaur dinosaurs](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/tyrannosaur-rex-size-comparison.jpg)

_This colorful diagram shows the size comparison of several tyrannosaurs, including \_Tyrannosaurus rex\_. These are known tyrannosaurs, and many more likely remain to be discovered._

  

## Fast Facts about Tyrannosaur Dinosaurs

Tyrannosaurs were a group of theropod dinosaurs that included everything from early, smaller-bodied hunters to the enormous apex predators of the Late Cretaceous. The most famous member is _Tyrannosaurus rex_, but it was only one branch of a much larger evolutionary story.

  

**Group:** Theropod dinosaurs within Tyrannosauroidea and Tyrannosauridae.   
  
**Best-known member:**_Tyrannosaurus rex_, the giant Late Cretaceous predator from western North America.   
  
**Distribution:** Mainly western North America (Laramidia) and Asia, with earlier tyrannosauroids known more broadly across Laurasia.   
  
**Time range:** Early tyrannosauroids appeared long before _T. rex_, while the largest tyrannosaurids dominated near the end of the Cretaceous.   
  
**Body size:** Early forms were relatively small, while later forms such as _T. rex_ and _Tarbosaurus_ reached giant size.   
  
**Major traits:** Large skulls, strong jaws, forward-facing eyes, powerful hind limbs, and reduced arms in the later giant forms.   
  
**Feathers:** Some early tyrannosauroids, such as _Yutyrannus_, had feathers or feather-like coverings. Later giant tyrannosaurs show scaly skin impressions.

  

  

* * *

## Tyrannosaur Distribution: Laramidia and Asia

Although _T. rex_ is the most famous tyrannosaur, it was not the only one. Several different tyrannosaurs lived during the Late Cretaceous, especially in western North America and Asia. In North America, the most important region was **Laramidia**, the western island continent separated from eastern North America by the Western Interior Seaway.

  
![Image 9: Late Cretaceous map showing tyrannosaur distribution in Laramidia and Asia](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/tyrannosaur-distribution-map-cretaceous.jpg)

_Approximate Late Cretaceous map showing tyrannosaur distribution. More tyrannosaur fossils will likely be found in Asia, northern Laramidia, and southern Laramidia as more areas are explored._

  

### Why are tyrannosaurs mostly found in Laramidia and Asia?

Late Cretaceous tyrannosaurids are best known from western North America and Asia. These regions were periodically connected by northern land routes, allowing dinosaur faunas to move between the continents. This helps explain why North American tyrannosaurs such as _T. rex_ and Asian tyrannosaurs such as _Tarbosaurus_ share so many similarities.

  

Other continents were more isolated during much of the Late Cretaceous. Europe was a series of islands, South America and Africa were separated by broad oceans, and Australia and Antarctica were far from the main tyrannosaur centers. This geographic isolation helps explain why giant tyrannosaurids are not found worldwide.

## Types of Tyrannosaur Dinosaurs

Tyrannosaurs belong within the coelurosaurian branch of theropod dinosaurs, the same broad group that also includes many feathered dinosaurs and the lineage that eventually led to birds. Early tyrannosauroids were generally smaller and more lightly built. Over time, some lineages evolved the massive skulls, bone-crushing teeth, and reduced arms seen in later tyrannosaurids.

  

The tyrannosaur fossil record shows tremendous diversity. Some species were adapted to warm southern environments, others lived in northern polar regions, and some Asian species looked remarkably similar to _T. rex_. The group continued evolving until the end-Cretaceous mass extinction brought their reign to an abrupt end.

## Tyrannosaurs of Laramidia

  

### _Lythronax argestes_ — The Southern King of Gore — South Laramidia — 80 Mya

![Image 12: Lythronax argestes tyrannosaur dinosaur on display at the Natural History Museum of Utah](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/tyrannosaur-dinosaur-lythronax-argestes.jpg)

_Reconstructed \_Lythronax argestes\_ on display at the [Natural History Museum of Utah](https://nhmu.utah.edu/). Credit: Mark Loewen / NHMU._

  

At about 80 million years old, _Lythronax argestes_ is one of the oldest known large tyrannosaurids. Its fossils come from Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument in Utah, which was part of southern Laramidia during the Late Cretaceous.

  

Although smaller than _T. rex_, _Lythronax_ already had many classic tyrannosaur traits, including a short, wide skull, robust teeth, forward-facing eyes, and reduced arms. This shows that several important tyrannosaur features evolved earlier than the final appearance of _Tyrannosaurus rex_.

  

* * *

  

### _Daspletosaurus torosus_ — Muscular Frightful Lizard — North Laramidia — 76 Mya

![Image 13: Reconstructed Daspletosaurus dinosaur specimen FMNH PR308 from Alberta](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/Field_Museum_Daspletosaurus_m.jpg)

_Reconstructed \_Daspletosaurus\_ specimen FMNH PR308 from the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta. Image credit: [A Stranger in the Alps](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/User:AStrangerintheAlps) (CC BY-SA 3.0)._

  

_Daspletosaurus torosus_ lived about 77 to 74 million years ago in northern Laramidia. It grew to roughly 30 feet in length and had a large skull, strong jaws, and small crests above the eyes.

  

This tyrannosaur lived alongside another large predator, _Gorgosaurus_. Having two large carnivorous theropods in the same region is unusual, and paleontologists have suggested they may have occupied different ecological niches or had partially separated geographic ranges.

  

* * *

  

### _Teratophoneus curriei_ — Monster Murderer — South Laramidia — 75 Mya

![Image 14: Skull reconstructions and cranial elements of Teratophoneus curriei from Loewen et al 2013](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/mark-a-loewen-tyrant-dinosaur-evolution-fig3.jpg)

_Figure from [Loewen et al. (2013)](https://dx.doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0079420) showing skull reconstructions and selected cranial elements of \_Teratophoneus curriei\_._

  

While _Daspletosaurus_ lived in northern Laramidia, _Teratophoneus curriei_ lived farther south in what is now Utah. Its fossils come from the Kaiparowits Formation, which is about 76 to 74 million years old.

  

_Teratophoneus_ was smaller than the giant tyrannosaurs that came later, and its skull was comparatively short. Differences between southern and northern tyrannosaurs suggest that Laramidia may have had regional dinosaur communities separated by geography, sea-level changes, or mountain-building events.

  
![Image 15: Skeletal reconstructions of Utah tyrannosaurs Lythronax and Teratophoneus](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/mark-a-loewen-tyrant-dinosaur-evolution-fig1.jpg)

_Skeletal reconstructions of Utah tyrannosaurs from Loewen et al. (2013), including \_Lythronax argestes\_ and \_Teratophoneus curriei\_._

  

* * *

  

### _Bistahieversor sealeyi_ — The Bistahi Destroyer — South Laramidia — 74 Mya

![Image 16: Comparison of adult and juvenile Bistahieversor sealeyi skulls](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/dinosaur-bistahieversor-sealeyi-carr-williamson-2010.jpg)

_Comparison of the adult holotype skull (NMMNH P-27469) and juvenile skull (P-25049) of \_Bistahieversor sealeyi\_. Figure from Carr and Williamson (2010)._

  

_Bistahieversor sealeyi_ lived about 74 million years ago in what is now New Mexico. At roughly 28 feet long, it was smaller than _T. rex_ but was one of the top predators of southern Laramidia at the time.

  

This tyrannosaur had several distinctive skull features, including an additional opening above the eye socket, a keel along the lower jaw, and a specialized jaw joint. These features show that southern Laramidian tyrannosaurs were evolving their own regional forms before the later rise of _Tyrannosaurus rex_.

  

* * *

  

### _Nanotyrannus lancensis_ — Dwarf Tyrant — Laramidia — 67 to 66 Mya

![Image 17: Cast of Jane, a small tyrannosaur specimen at the Carnegie Museum of Natural History](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/tyrannosaur-jane-dinosaur.jpg)

_Cast of “Jane” (BMRP 2002.4.1), a small tyrannosaur specimen central to the long-running \_Nanotyrannus\_ debate._

  

_Nanotyrannus lancensis_ has long been controversial. For decades, many paleontologists debated whether it was a separate tyrannosaur or simply a juvenile _Tyrannosaurus rex_. Recent research on the famous Dueling Dinosaurs specimen supports _Nanotyrannus_ as a distinct, fully grown tyrannosaur rather than a teenage _T. rex_.

  

Compared to _T. rex_, _Nanotyrannus_ was smaller, more lightly built, and more agile, with proportionally longer arms and a higher tooth count. If these interpretations continue to hold, the end of the Cretaceous was more ecologically complex than once thought, with multiple tyrannosaur predators sharing the same ecosystems.

  

For more detail, see the main [T. rex page section on _Nanotyrannus_ vs. juvenile _T. rex_](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/tyrannosaurus.htm#juvenile).

  

* * *

  

### _Tyrannosaurus rex_ — Tyrant Lizard King — Laramidia — 67 to 66 Mya

![Image 18: Tyrannosaurus rex dinosaurs on display at the Carnegie Museum of Natural History](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/t-rex-dinosaurs.jpg)

_\_Tyrannosaurus rex\_ dinosaurs on display at the Carnegie Museum of Natural History in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania._

  

Reaching lengths of more than 40 feet, _Tyrannosaurus rex_ was the largest and most famous of the tyrannosaurs. It represents the peak of the giant tyrannosaur body plan: a massive skull, bone-crushing jaws, forward-facing eyes, powerful hind limbs, and reduced but muscular arms.

  

_T. rex_ lived across Laramidia near the very end of the Cretaceous. Fossils are found from Canada through the western United States, including famous formations such as the Hell Creek and Lance formations. For a complete guide, visit the [main _Tyrannosaurus rex_ page](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/tyrannosaurus.htm).

  

* * *

  

### _Nanuqsaurus hoglundi_ — Polar Bear Lizard — Polar Laramidia — 69 Mya

![Image 19: Nanuqsaurus hoglundi holotype skull and jaw fragments](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/nanuqsaurus-tyrannosaur-fig3-fiorillo2014.jpg)

_Figure from [Fiorillo and Tykoski (2014)](https://dx.doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0091287) showing the \_Nanuqsaurus hoglundi\_ holotype specimen, including skull and jaw fragments._

  

_Nanuqsaurus hoglundi_ is a polar tyrannosaur from the Prince Creek Formation of northern Alaska. Its name comes from “nanuq,” an Iñupiat word for polar bear. The fossils are about 69 million years old and represent one of the most northern tyrannosaurs known.

  

This animal was smaller than an average _T. rex_. Its reduced size may reflect adaptation to a high-latitude environment with long winter darkness and seasonal food stress. The discovery of _Nanuqsaurus_ shows that tyrannosaurs were able to thrive in a wide range of Late Cretaceous environments, including polar regions.

  

* * *

  

## Tyrannosaurs of Asia

  

### _Tarbosaurus bataar_ — Alarming Lizard Hero — Asia — 70 Mya

![Image 20: Tarbosaurus bataar dinosaur skeleton from Mongolia](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/800px-MEPAN_tarbosaurus_bataar.jpg)

_\_Tarbosaurus bataar\_ skeleton displayed at the Muzeum Ewolucji PAN w Warszawie. Image credit: [Hiuppo](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/User:Hiuppo) (CC BY-SA 3.0)._

  

_Tarbosaurus bataar_ was the giant tyrannosaur of Mongolia and China. It looked very similar to _T. rex_ and reached comparable size, though its skull was generally narrower and its arms were even shorter.

  

At the end of the Cretaceous, _Tarbosaurus_ was the apex predator of its Asian ecosystems, while _T. rex_ filled a similar role in Laramidia. Juvenile, subadult, and adult _Tarbosaurus_ specimens have helped paleontologists better understand how large tyrannosaurs changed as they grew.

  

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ucE-6mEgy1E)

_**Video showing the growth series of \_Tarbosaurus\_, a close relative of \_T. rex\_.**_

  

* * *

  

### _Yutyrannus huali_ — Feathered Tyrant — Asia — 124 Mya

![Image 21: Illustration of Yutyrannus huali, a large feathered tyrannosauroid](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/Yutyrannus2.jpg)

_Illustration of \_Yutyrannus huali\_, a giant feathered early tyrannosauroid that lived in a cooler climate than \_T. rex\_. Illustration by Lida Xing and Yi Liu._

  

_Yutyrannus huali_ was not a late giant tyrannosaurid like _T. rex_, but it is an important early tyrannosauroid. It lived about 124 million years ago in China and is famous because fossils preserve feather impressions.

  

At nearly 30 feet long, _Yutyrannus_ is among the largest theropods known with direct evidence of feathers or feather-like filaments. These structures may have helped with insulation in a cooler Early Cretaceous climate. However, this does not prove that adult _T. rex_ was feathered, because later tyrannosaur skin impressions show scales in the areas where feathers might otherwise be expected.

  

* * *

  

### _Zhuchengtyrannus magnus_ — Great Tyrant of Zhucheng — Asia — 74 Mya

![Image 22: Lower jaw of Zhuchengtyrannus magnus, a large Asian tyrannosaur](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/zhuchengtyrannus-dinosaur-hone-2011.jpg)

_Lower jaw of \_Zhuchengtyrannus magnus\_. Image from [Hone et al. (2011)](https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.cretres.2011.03.005)._

  

_Zhuchengtyrannus magnus_ is a large tyrannosaur from China dating to about 73 to 74 million years ago. It is known from jaw material found at the Zangjiazhuang quarry in Zhucheng, China.

  

Although the fossil material is limited, _Zhuchengtyrannus_ appears to have been a large tyrannosaur, possibly approaching the size of _Tarbosaurus_. More complete fossils from the region may eventually clarify how this animal fit into Asian tyrannosaur evolution.

## Origins of Tyrannosaurs

The giant tyrannosaurids of the Late Cretaceous were the end result of a long evolutionary history. Early tyrannosauroids were much smaller than _T. rex_ and lived long before the final Cretaceous ecosystems of Laramidia and Asia. For much of their early history, they were not the dominant predators.

  

Earlier in the Mesozoic, other large theropods such as allosauroids and carcharodontosaurids often occupied top-predator roles. As these groups declined or disappeared in some regions, tyrannosaurs expanded into the apex predator niche. Over time, some lineages evolved larger bodies, stronger skulls, forward-facing eyes, bone-crushing teeth, and reduced arms.

  

By the Late Cretaceous, tyrannosaurs had become the dominant large predators in Asia and Laramidia. The final giant forms, including _Tarbosaurus_ and _Tyrannosaurus rex_, represent one of the most specialized predator lineages in dinosaur history.

## FAQs: Tyrannosaur Dinosaurs - Frequently Asked Questions

Quick answers to common questions about tyrannosaur dinosaurs, including _T. rex_, _Nanotyrannus_, _Tarbosaurus_, _Yutyrannus_, and the evolution of giant tyrannosaur predators.

  

*   **What is a tyrannosaur?**  
 A tyrannosaur is a theropod dinosaur belonging to the broader tyrannosauroid lineage. Famous late members include _Tyrannosaurus rex_, _Tarbosaurus_, _Daspletosaurus_, _Albertosaurus_, and other large predatory dinosaurs.   
See: Types of Tyrannosaurs 
*   **Was Tyrannosaurus rex the only tyrannosaur?**  
 No. _Tyrannosaurus rex_ was only one member of a larger tyrannosaur group. Other tyrannosaurs include _Lythronax_, _Daspletosaurus_, _Teratophoneus_, _Bistahieversor_, _Nanuqsaurus_, _Tarbosaurus_, _Zhuchengtyrannus_, and _Nanotyrannus_.   
See: Types of Tyrannosaurs 

*   **Where have tyrannosaur fossils been found?**  
 Tyrannosaur fossils are best known from western North America, especially the ancient landmass Laramidia, and from eastern Asia, including Mongolia and China.   
See: Tyrannosaur Distribution 
*   **What is Laramidia?**  
 Laramidia was the western island continent of North America during the Late Cretaceous, separated from eastern North America by the Western Interior Seaway. Several famous tyrannosaurs evolved there.   
See: Tyrannosaur Distribution 
*   **Did tyrannosaurs originate in Asia or North America?**  
 Early tyrannosauroids were widespread across Laurasia, with important fossils known from Asia, Europe, and North America. The giant Late Cretaceous tyrannosaurids later became especially successful in Asia and Laramidia.   
See: Origins of Tyrannosaurs 
*   **Were all tyrannosaurs giant predators?**  
 No. Early tyrannosauroids were much smaller and more lightly built than _Tyrannosaurus rex_. The gigantic, bone-crushing body plan evolved later in the history of the group.   
See: Origins of Tyrannosaurs 
*   **Did tyrannosaurs have feathers?**  
 Some early tyrannosauroids, including _Yutyrannus_, had feather-like coverings. Later giant tyrannosaurs such as _Tyrannosaurus rex_ show scaly skin impressions, suggesting adults were mostly or fully scaly.   
See: Yutyrannus 
*   **Is Nanotyrannus a juvenile T. rex?**  
 Recent research supports _Nanotyrannus_ as a distinct tyrannosaur rather than a juvenile _Tyrannosaurus rex_. This means multiple tyrannosaur predators may have lived together near the end of the Cretaceous.   
See: Nanotyrannus 
*   **What was the Asian version of T. rex?**  
_Tarbosaurus bataar_ is often described as the Asian counterpart of _Tyrannosaurus rex_. It lived in Mongolia and China near the end of the Cretaceous and was one of Asia's largest predatory dinosaurs.   
See: Tarbosaurus 
*   **Why are tyrannosaurs important to paleontology?**  
 Tyrannosaurs help paleontologists understand predator evolution, continental connections between Asia and North America, dinosaur growth, ecosystem structure, and how giant apex predators evolved before the end-Cretaceous extinction.   
See: Types of Tyrannosaurs

# Types of Tyrannosaur Dinosaurs and the Origins of T. rex

There was much more to the tyrannosaur family than _Tyrannosaurus rex_. Learn about the different types of tyrannosaur dinosaurs, where they lived, how they evolved, and how early feathered relatives eventually led to the giant bone-crushing predators of the Late Cretaceous.

_Article written by: [Jayson Kowinsky, The Fossilguy](https://www.fossilguy.com/author.htm)_

| Published August 10, 2015 (Updated: 01/27/2026)

![Image 8: Tyrannosaur size comparison showing T. rex and other tyrannosaur dinosaurs](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/tyrannosaur-rex-size-comparison.jpg)

_This colorful diagram shows the size comparison of several tyrannosaurs, including \_Tyrannosaurus rex\_. These are known tyrannosaurs, and many more likely remain to be discovered._

  

## Fast Facts about Tyrannosaur Dinosaurs

Tyrannosaurs were a group of theropod dinosaurs that included everything from early, smaller-bodied hunters to the enormous apex predators of the Late Cretaceous. The most famous member is _Tyrannosaurus rex_, but it was only one branch of a much larger evolutionary story.

  

**Group:** Theropod dinosaurs within Tyrannosauroidea and Tyrannosauridae.   
  
**Best-known member:**_Tyrannosaurus rex_, the giant Late Cretaceous predator from western North America.   
  
**Distribution:** Mainly western North America (Laramidia) and Asia, with earlier tyrannosauroids known more broadly across Laurasia.   
  
**Time range:** Early tyrannosauroids appeared long before _T. rex_, while the largest tyrannosaurids dominated near the end of the Cretaceous.   
  
**Body size:** Early forms were relatively small, while later forms such as _T. rex_ and _Tarbosaurus_ reached giant size.   
  
**Major traits:** Large skulls, strong jaws, forward-facing eyes, powerful hind limbs, and reduced arms in the later giant forms.   
  
**Feathers:** Some early tyrannosauroids, such as _Yutyrannus_, had feathers or feather-like coverings. Later giant tyrannosaurs show scaly skin impressions.

  

  

* * *

## Tyrannosaur Distribution: Laramidia and Asia

Although _T. rex_ is the most famous tyrannosaur, it was not the only one. Several different tyrannosaurs lived during the Late Cretaceous, especially in western North America and Asia. In North America, the most important region was **Laramidia**, the western island continent separated from eastern North America by the Western Interior Seaway.

  
![Image 9: Late Cretaceous map showing tyrannosaur distribution in Laramidia and Asia](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/tyrannosaur-distribution-map-cretaceous.jpg)

_Approximate Late Cretaceous map showing tyrannosaur distribution. More tyrannosaur fossils will likely be found in Asia, northern Laramidia, and southern Laramidia as more areas are explored._

  

### Why are tyrannosaurs mostly found in Laramidia and Asia?

Late Cretaceous tyrannosaurids are best known from western North America and Asia. These regions were periodically connected by northern land routes, allowing dinosaur faunas to move between the continents. This helps explain why North American tyrannosaurs such as _T. rex_ and Asian tyrannosaurs such as _Tarbosaurus_ share so many similarities.

  

Other continents were more isolated during much of the Late Cretaceous. Europe was a series of islands, South America and Africa were separated by broad oceans, and Australia and Antarctica were far from the main tyrannosaur centers. This geographic isolation helps explain why giant tyrannosaurids are not found worldwide.

## Types of Tyrannosaur Dinosaurs

Tyrannosaurs belong within the coelurosaurian branch of theropod dinosaurs, the same broad group that also includes many feathered dinosaurs and the lineage that eventually led to birds. Early tyrannosauroids were generally smaller and more lightly built. Over time, some lineages evolved the massive skulls, bone-crushing teeth, and reduced arms seen in later tyrannosaurids.

  

The tyrannosaur fossil record shows tremendous diversity. Some species were adapted to warm southern environments, others lived in northern polar regions, and some Asian species looked remarkably similar to _T. rex_. The group continued evolving until the end-Cretaceous mass extinction brought their reign to an abrupt end.

## Tyrannosaurs of Laramidia

  

### _Lythronax argestes_ — The Southern King of Gore — South Laramidia — 80 Mya

![Image 12: Lythronax argestes tyrannosaur dinosaur on display at the Natural History Museum of Utah](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/tyrannosaur-dinosaur-lythronax-argestes.jpg)

_Reconstructed \_Lythronax argestes\_ on display at the [Natural History Museum of Utah](https://nhmu.utah.edu/). Credit: Mark Loewen / NHMU._

  

At about 80 million years old, _Lythronax argestes_ is one of the oldest known large tyrannosaurids. Its fossils come from Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument in Utah, which was part of southern Laramidia during the Late Cretaceous.

  

Although smaller than _T. rex_, _Lythronax_ already had many classic tyrannosaur traits, including a short, wide skull, robust teeth, forward-facing eyes, and reduced arms. This shows that several important tyrannosaur features evolved earlier than the final appearance of _Tyrannosaurus rex_.

  

* * *

  

### _Daspletosaurus torosus_ — Muscular Frightful Lizard — North Laramidia — 76 Mya

![Image 13: Reconstructed Daspletosaurus dinosaur specimen FMNH PR308 from Alberta](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/Field_Museum_Daspletosaurus_m.jpg)

_Reconstructed \_Daspletosaurus\_ specimen FMNH PR308 from the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta. Image credit: [A Stranger in the Alps](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/User:AStrangerintheAlps) (CC BY-SA 3.0)._

  

_Daspletosaurus torosus_ lived about 77 to 74 million years ago in northern Laramidia. It grew to roughly 30 feet in length and had a large skull, strong jaws, and small crests above the eyes.

  

This tyrannosaur lived alongside another large predator, _Gorgosaurus_. Having two large carnivorous theropods in the same region is unusual, and paleontologists have suggested they may have occupied different ecological niches or had partially separated geographic ranges.

  

* * *

  

### _Teratophoneus curriei_ — Monster Murderer — South Laramidia — 75 Mya

![Image 14: Skull reconstructions and cranial elements of Teratophoneus curriei from Loewen et al 2013](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/mark-a-loewen-tyrant-dinosaur-evolution-fig3.jpg)

_Figure from [Loewen et al. (2013)](https://dx.doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0079420) showing skull reconstructions and selected cranial elements of \_Teratophoneus curriei\_._

  

While _Daspletosaurus_ lived in northern Laramidia, _Teratophoneus curriei_ lived farther south in what is now Utah. Its fossils come from the Kaiparowits Formation, which is about 76 to 74 million years old.

  

_Teratophoneus_ was smaller than the giant tyrannosaurs that came later, and its skull was comparatively short. Differences between southern and northern tyrannosaurs suggest that Laramidia may have had regional dinosaur communities separated by geography, sea-level changes, or mountain-building events.

  
![Image 15: Skeletal reconstructions of Utah tyrannosaurs Lythronax and Teratophoneus](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/mark-a-loewen-tyrant-dinosaur-evolution-fig1.jpg)

_Skeletal reconstructions of Utah tyrannosaurs from Loewen et al. (2013), including \_Lythronax argestes\_ and \_Teratophoneus curriei\_._

  

* * *

  

### _Bistahieversor sealeyi_ — The Bistahi Destroyer — South Laramidia — 74 Mya

![Image 16: Comparison of adult and juvenile Bistahieversor sealeyi skulls](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/dinosaur-bistahieversor-sealeyi-carr-williamson-2010.jpg)

_Comparison of the adult holotype skull (NMMNH P-27469) and juvenile skull (P-25049) of \_Bistahieversor sealeyi\_. Figure from Carr and Williamson (2010)._

  

_Bistahieversor sealeyi_ lived about 74 million years ago in what is now New Mexico. At roughly 28 feet long, it was smaller than _T. rex_ but was one of the top predators of southern Laramidia at the time.

  

This tyrannosaur had several distinctive skull features, including an additional opening above the eye socket, a keel along the lower jaw, and a specialized jaw joint. These features show that southern Laramidian tyrannosaurs were evolving their own regional forms before the later rise of _Tyrannosaurus rex_.

  

* * *

  

### _Nanotyrannus lancensis_ — Dwarf Tyrant — Laramidia — 67 to 66 Mya

![Image 17: Cast of Jane, a small tyrannosaur specimen at the Carnegie Museum of Natural History](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/tyrannosaur-jane-dinosaur.jpg)

_Cast of “Jane” (BMRP 2002.4.1), a small tyrannosaur specimen central to the long-running \_Nanotyrannus\_ debate._

  

_Nanotyrannus lancensis_ has long been controversial. For decades, many paleontologists debated whether it was a separate tyrannosaur or simply a juvenile _Tyrannosaurus rex_. Recent research on the famous Dueling Dinosaurs specimen supports _Nanotyrannus_ as a distinct, fully grown tyrannosaur rather than a teenage _T. rex_.

  

Compared to _T. rex_, _Nanotyrannus_ was smaller, more lightly built, and more agile, with proportionally longer arms and a higher tooth count. If these interpretations continue to hold, the end of the Cretaceous was more ecologically complex than once thought, with multiple tyrannosaur predators sharing the same ecosystems.

  

For more detail, see the main [T. rex page section on _Nanotyrannus_ vs. juvenile _T. rex_](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/tyrannosaurus.htm#juvenile).

  

* * *

  

### _Tyrannosaurus rex_ — Tyrant Lizard King — Laramidia — 67 to 66 Mya

![Image 18: Tyrannosaurus rex dinosaurs on display at the Carnegie Museum of Natural History](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/t-rex-dinosaurs.jpg)

_\_Tyrannosaurus rex\_ dinosaurs on display at the Carnegie Museum of Natural History in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania._

  

Reaching lengths of more than 40 feet, _Tyrannosaurus rex_ was the largest and most famous of the tyrannosaurs. It represents the peak of the giant tyrannosaur body plan: a massive skull, bone-crushing jaws, forward-facing eyes, powerful hind limbs, and reduced but muscular arms.

  

_T. rex_ lived across Laramidia near the very end of the Cretaceous. Fossils are found from Canada through the western United States, including famous formations such as the Hell Creek and Lance formations. For a complete guide, visit the [main _Tyrannosaurus rex_ page](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/tyrannosaurus.htm).

  

* * *

  

### _Nanuqsaurus hoglundi_ — Polar Bear Lizard — Polar Laramidia — 69 Mya

![Image 19: Nanuqsaurus hoglundi holotype skull and jaw fragments](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/nanuqsaurus-tyrannosaur-fig3-fiorillo2014.jpg)

_Figure from [Fiorillo and Tykoski (2014)](https://dx.doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0091287) showing the \_Nanuqsaurus hoglundi\_ holotype specimen, including skull and jaw fragments._

  

_Nanuqsaurus hoglundi_ is a polar tyrannosaur from the Prince Creek Formation of northern Alaska. Its name comes from “nanuq,” an Iñupiat word for polar bear. The fossils are about 69 million years old and represent one of the most northern tyrannosaurs known.

  

This animal was smaller than an average _T. rex_. Its reduced size may reflect adaptation to a high-latitude environment with long winter darkness and seasonal food stress. The discovery of _Nanuqsaurus_ shows that tyrannosaurs were able to thrive in a wide range of Late Cretaceous environments, including polar regions.

  

* * *

  

## Tyrannosaurs of Asia

  

### _Tarbosaurus bataar_ — Alarming Lizard Hero — Asia — 70 Mya

![Image 20: Tarbosaurus bataar dinosaur skeleton from Mongolia](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/800px-MEPAN_tarbosaurus_bataar.jpg)

_\_Tarbosaurus bataar\_ skeleton displayed at the Muzeum Ewolucji PAN w Warszawie. Image credit: [Hiuppo](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/User:Hiuppo) (CC BY-SA 3.0)._

  

_Tarbosaurus bataar_ was the giant tyrannosaur of Mongolia and China. It looked very similar to _T. rex_ and reached comparable size, though its skull was generally narrower and its arms were even shorter.

  

At the end of the Cretaceous, _Tarbosaurus_ was the apex predator of its Asian ecosystems, while _T. rex_ filled a similar role in Laramidia. Juvenile, subadult, and adult _Tarbosaurus_ specimens have helped paleontologists better understand how large tyrannosaurs changed as they grew.

  

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ucE-6mEgy1E)

_**Video showing the growth series of \_Tarbosaurus\_, a close relative of \_T. rex\_.**_

  

* * *

  

### _Yutyrannus huali_ — Feathered Tyrant — Asia — 124 Mya

![Image 21: Illustration of Yutyrannus huali, a large feathered tyrannosauroid](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/Yutyrannus2.jpg)

_Illustration of \_Yutyrannus huali\_, a giant feathered early tyrannosauroid that lived in a cooler climate than \_T. rex\_. Illustration by Lida Xing and Yi Liu._

  

_Yutyrannus huali_ was not a late giant tyrannosaurid like _T. rex_, but it is an important early tyrannosauroid. It lived about 124 million years ago in China and is famous because fossils preserve feather impressions.

  

At nearly 30 feet long, _Yutyrannus_ is among the largest theropods known with direct evidence of feathers or feather-like filaments. These structures may have helped with insulation in a cooler Early Cretaceous climate. However, this does not prove that adult _T. rex_ was feathered, because later tyrannosaur skin impressions show scales in the areas where feathers might otherwise be expected.

  

* * *

  

### _Zhuchengtyrannus magnus_ — Great Tyrant of Zhucheng — Asia — 74 Mya

![Image 22: Lower jaw of Zhuchengtyrannus magnus, a large Asian tyrannosaur](https://www.fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/dinosaur/tyrannosaurus/zhuchengtyrannus-dinosaur-hone-2011.jpg)

_Lower jaw of \_Zhuchengtyrannus magnus\_. Image from [Hone et al. (2011)](https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.cretres.2011.03.005)._

  

_Zhuchengtyrannus magnus_ is a large tyrannosaur from China dating to about 73 to 74 million years ago. It is known from jaw material found at the Zangjiazhuang quarry in Zhucheng, China.

  

Although the fossil material is limited, _Zhuchengtyrannus_ appears to have been a large tyrannosaur, possibly approaching the size of _Tarbosaurus_. More complete fossils from the region may eventually clarify how this animal fit into Asian tyrannosaur evolution.

## Origins of Tyrannosaurs

The giant tyrannosaurids of the Late Cretaceous were the end result of a long evolutionary history. Early tyrannosauroids were much smaller than _T. rex_ and lived long before the final Cretaceous ecosystems of Laramidia and Asia. For much of their early history, they were not the dominant predators.

  

Earlier in the Mesozoic, other large theropods such as allosauroids and carcharodontosaurids often occupied top-predator roles. As these groups declined or disappeared in some regions, tyrannosaurs expanded into the apex predator niche. Over time, some lineages evolved larger bodies, stronger skulls, forward-facing eyes, bone-crushing teeth, and reduced arms.

  

By the Late Cretaceous, tyrannosaurs had become the dominant large predators in Asia and Laramidia. The final giant forms, including _Tarbosaurus_ and _Tyrannosaurus rex_, represent one of the most specialized predator lineages in dinosaur history.

## FAQs: Tyrannosaur Dinosaurs - Frequently Asked Questions

Quick answers to common questions about tyrannosaur dinosaurs, including _T. rex_, _Nanotyrannus_, _Tarbosaurus_, _Yutyrannus_, and the evolution of giant tyrannosaur predators.

  

*   **What is a tyrannosaur?**  
 A tyrannosaur is a theropod dinosaur belonging to the broader tyrannosauroid lineage. Famous late members include _Tyrannosaurus rex_, _Tarbosaurus_, _Daspletosaurus_, _Albertosaurus_, and other large predatory dinosaurs.   
See: Types of Tyrannosaurs 
*   **Was Tyrannosaurus rex the only tyrannosaur?**  
 No. _Tyrannosaurus rex_ was only one member of a larger tyrannosaur group. Other tyrannosaurs include _Lythronax_, _Daspletosaurus_, _Teratophoneus_, _Bistahieversor_, _Nanuqsaurus_, _Tarbosaurus_, _Zhuchengtyrannus_, and _Nanotyrannus_.   
See: Types of Tyrannosaurs 

*   **Where have tyrannosaur fossils been found?**  
 Tyrannosaur fossils are best known from western North America, especially the ancient landmass Laramidia, and from eastern Asia, including Mongolia and China.   
See: Tyrannosaur Distribution 
*   **What is Laramidia?**  
 Laramidia was the western island continent of North America during the Late Cretaceous, separated from eastern North America by the Western Interior Seaway. Several famous tyrannosaurs evolved there.   
See: Tyrannosaur Distribution 
*   **Did tyrannosaurs originate in Asia or North America?**  
 Early tyrannosauroids were widespread across Laurasia, with important fossils known from Asia, Europe, and North America. The giant Late Cretaceous tyrannosaurids later became especially successful in Asia and Laramidia.   
See: Origins of Tyrannosaurs 
*   **Were all tyrannosaurs giant predators?**  
 No. Early tyrannosauroids were much smaller and more lightly built than _Tyrannosaurus rex_. The gigantic, bone-crushing body plan evolved later in the history of the group.   
See: Origins of Tyrannosaurs 
*   **Did tyrannosaurs have feathers?**  
 Some early tyrannosauroids, including _Yutyrannus_, had feather-like coverings. Later giant tyrannosaurs such as _Tyrannosaurus rex_ show scaly skin impressions, suggesting adults were mostly or fully scaly.   
See: Yutyrannus 
*   **Is Nanotyrannus a juvenile T. rex?**  
 Recent research supports _Nanotyrannus_ as a distinct tyrannosaur rather than a juvenile _Tyrannosaurus rex_. This means multiple tyrannosaur predators may have lived together near the end of the Cretaceous.   
See: Nanotyrannus 
*   **What was the Asian version of T. rex?**  
_Tarbosaurus bataar_ is often described as the Asian counterpart of _Tyrannosaurus rex_. It lived in Mongolia and China near the end of the Cretaceous and was one of Asia's largest predatory dinosaurs.   
See: Tarbosaurus 
*   **Why are tyrannosaurs important to paleontology?**  
 Tyrannosaurs help paleontologists understand predator evolution, continental connections between Asia and North America, dinosaur growth, ecosystem structure, and how giant apex predators evolved before the end-Cretaceous extinction.   
See: Types of Tyrannosaurs

Approximate distribution range of _Tyrannosaurus rex_

_**Tyrannosaurus**_ (Greek for "tyrant lizard") is an extinct genus of [tyrannosaurid](https://dinopedia.fandom.com/wiki/Tyrannosauridae "Tyrannosauridae")[theropod](https://dinopedia.fandom.com/wiki/Theropod "Theropod")[dinosaur](https://dinopedia.fandom.com/wiki/Dinosaur "Dinosaur") that flourished during the [Maastrichtian age](https://dinopedia.fandom.com/wiki/Maastrichtian "Maastrichtian") of the [Late Cretaceous](https://dinopedia.fandom.com/wiki/Late_Cretaceous "Late Cretaceous"), 72-66 million years ago. The [type species](https://dinopedia.fandom.com/wiki/Type_species "Type species") is _T. rex_ (Greek for "Tyrant Lizard King"), named in 1905. A second, older species; _T. mcraeensis_ (Meaning "Tyrant Lizard from M Ras") named in 2024, although its validity is disputed. Others have been suggested but are considered invalid, these include _Tyrannosaurus regina_ and _Tyrannosaurus imperator_.

Ever since its discovery, _Tyrannosaurus_ has become one of, if not the most popular non-avian dinosaur. Since its discovery, over 50 individuals of this taxon have been unearthed. The most complete specimen of the _T. rex_ was nicknamed "Sue" (located at Chicago's [Field Museum of Natural History](https://dinopedia.fandom.com/wiki/Field_Museum_of_Natural_History "Field Museum of Natural History"), which is roughly 90% complete), measuring approximately 12.3+ meters (40+ feet) in length, around 3.9 meters (12.8 feet) high at the hips, and an average weight of 10 tonnes, making it amongst the largest terrestrial carnivores & theropods that ever existed on Earth. There are other specimens estimated to be larger than Sue, but information regarding these specimens is debated. However, one specimen, known as "Scotty", measured 13.2 meters (43 feet) in length, stood 4 (13.12 feet) meters at the hips, and weighed nearly 10 tonnes, making _Tyrannosaurus_ currently the biggest theropod and fully-terrestrial carnivore known to science. Additionally, recent research suggests that _Tyrannosaurus_ may potentially have been able to grow larger than previously thought, potentially growing to 14 m (48 feet) long, growing to stand 5 m (16 feet) tall, and weigh around 15 tonnes.

Fossils have been uncovered in [North America](https://dinopedia.fandom.com/wiki/North_America "North America"), primarily in North and South Dakota, Texas, Montana, Colorado, Wyoming, and Saskatchewan within a depositional formation known as the "Hell Creek". It was among the last non-avian dinosaurs to live prior to the [K-Pg mass extinction event](https://dinopedia.fandom.com/wiki/K-Pg_Extinction "K-Pg Extinction").

A rather recent, although controversial study indicates that there could be three differentiated and varied species of _Tyrannosaurus_ and proposed two new species: _Tyrannosaurus imperator_ and _Tyrannosaurus regina_.[[1]](https://dinopedia.fandom.com/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-:0-1)[[2]](https://dinopedia.fandom.com/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-2) They are considered as invalid by most paleontologists, because the difference between these species can be explained with either individual variation or sexual dimorphism.
